clinicalPearls: A chronic inflammatory disease of the axial skeleton, encompassing ankylosing spondylitis (radiographic) and non-radiographic forms
The hallmark is inflammatory back pain: insidious onset before middle age, morning stiffness, improvement with exercise and not with rest, and night pain
It is strongly associated with HLA-B27 and with sacroiliitis on imaging
Extra-articular features include acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease
MRI detects active sacroiliitis before radiographic changes appear, enabling earlier diagnosis
Management combines exercise and NSAIDs with biologic therapy (TNF or IL-17 inhibitors) for active disease
reference.pathophysiology: Axial spondyloarthritis is an immune-mediated inflammatory disorder centred on the entheses and sacroiliac joints, in which inflammation at sites of ligament and tendon insertion is followed by reactive new bone formation. Genetic susceptibility, especially HLA-B27, and dysregulated innate and adaptive immunity involving the interleukin-23/17 axis drive the process. Over time, inflammation of the spine and sacroiliac joints can lead to syndesmophyte formation, ankylosis and loss of spinal mobility, while shared immunopathology explains the associated uveitis, psoriasis and bowel inflammation.
additionalInvestigations: Assessment of inflammatory back pain features
MRI of the sacroiliac joints for active inflammation
Radiographs of the sacroiliac joints and spine
Inflammatory markers and screening for extra-articular disease
redFlags: Features suggesting infective sacroiliitis or malignancy
Rapid loss of spinal mobility or spinal fracture in ankylosed spine
Cauda equina syndrome (rare, in long-standing disease)
reference.prognosis: Course is variable; early diagnosis and modern therapy can control symptoms and improve function, though some progress to spinal ankylosis with disability.
pitfalls: Dismissing chronic back pain in a young adult as mechanical
Relying on radiographs alone and missing early disease detectable on MRI
Overlooking extra-articular clues such as uveitis
Forgetting the high fracture risk of an ankylosed spine after trauma
management: Structured exercise and physiotherapy to preserve spinal mobility, posture and function form the cornerstone of management
Use NSAIDs as first-line pharmacotherapy for inflammatory pain and stiffness
For active disease refractory to NSAIDs, escalate to biologic therapy with a TNF inhibitor or IL-17 inhibitor, or a JAK inhibitor as an alternative
Reserve conventional DMARDs such as sulfasalazine for peripheral arthritis, as they do not control axial disease
Identify and co-manage extra-articular disease including acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease with the relevant specialists
Monitor disease activity and function with validated indices, and screen for and treat osteoporosis and cardiovascular risk while remaining alert to fracture through the rigid ankylosed spine
Coordinate long-term care through rheumatology and refer for physiotherapy and, where deformity is severe, spinal surgery
